part_title: EBS Availability-Zone Scope, Volume Families and gp3 Performance

scenes.title: EBS is persistent block storage within one AZ
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches ebs is persistent block storage within one az through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Trace an EC2 instance attaching an EBS volume in the same Availability Zone
Explain detach and reattach within that AZ versus snapshot-assisted relocation to another AZ
Compare deletion-on-termination and EBS throughput constraints to instance lifecycle
scenes.visual_example: An instance is replaced after failure and its retained EBS volume can be reattached to a compatible machine in the same AZ; restoring in another AZ needs a snapshot and new volume.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Volume persistence and Availability Zone placement are separate decisions.
scenes.narration: This slide introduces EBS as persistent network-attached block storage for Amazon EC2. Follow the connection from an instance to a volume inside the same Availability Zone. Most ordinary EBS volumes attach to one instance at a time; Multi-Attach is an explicit io1 or io2 capability with its own application coordination requirements. Next, look at the migration path. A detached volume can be reattached safely within its Availability Zone, but it cannot simply span Availability Zones. To restore in another zone, create a snapshot and provision a new volume in the destination zone. Finally, consider the lifecycle. The Delete on termination setting determines whether a volume can survive instance termination, and increasing volume size or performance may still require operating-system filesystem work and a suitable instance EBS bandwidth ceiling. For an important server, verify the retained volume, attachment and recovery procedure before assuming instance replacement will restore service.

scenes.title: EBS: choose the disk for the access pattern
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches ebs: choose the disk for the access pattern through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Compare general-purpose gp2 and gp3 SSD options for ordinary application workloads
Explain provisioned IOPS io1 and io2 where predictable random I/O matters
Distinguish sequential-throughput st1 and cold sc1 HDD classes, including boot restrictions
scenes.visual_example: A busy transactional database may justify io2, while large sequential analytics reads might favor st1; boot disks should use a supported SSD class.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The volume type follows I/O behavior rather than capacity alone.
scenes.narration: This slide is a selection comparison rather than a single sequential data flow. In the first panel, general-purpose SSD volumes, including gp2 and gp3, support common boot disks, application servers and balanced transactional workloads. gp3 offers independent capacity and provisioned performance controls within service limits. In the next panel, io1 and io2 target workloads with stronger sustained IOPS requirements; io2 Block Express offers higher-end performance characteristics, but the instance and application must also support the desired rate. On the third panel, throughput-oriented HDD classes are a different choice. st1 favors frequent sequential access while sc1 suits colder, less frequently accessed throughput workloads; neither is suitable as a boot volume. Suppose an architect must choose storage for a high-transaction database and a large sequential log-processing job. They may need different volume families even if both datasets occupy similar space. Always evaluate IOPS, I/O size, throughput, latency and price rather than choosing by gigabyte capacity alone.

scenes.title: gp2 and gp3 separate capacity from performance differently
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches gp2 and gp3 separate capacity from performance differently through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Read the gp2 credit-based burst behavior and its connection to capacity
Contrast gp3's independent baseline and adjustable IOPS and throughput settings
Check io2 and instance-level latency limits before choosing expensive performance
scenes.visual_example: A small gp2 volume experiencing sustained random I/O might run down burst credits; moving to appropriately provisioned gp3 can decouple performance from purchased capacity.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Buying more storage is not always the right way to buy I/O performance.
scenes.narration: This diagram emphasizes that storage capacity and performance are not the same quantity. The first panel illustrates gp2, where performance is related to capacity and smaller volumes rely on I/O credits for burst behavior. A workload with sustained random I/O can see performance change when those credits are exhausted. In the second panel, gp3 provides a baseline and lets the architect configure additional IOPS or throughput within supported limits without increasing capacity simply to chase I/O performance. The last panel introduces io2 as a choice for demanding applications, but even a fast EBS volume must work through the instance's bandwidth and IOPS ceilings. Consider a small but busy database volume. Increasing its gigabytes may be wasteful compared with selecting appropriate gp3 performance settings, while a genuinely latency-sensitive system may warrant io2 after testing. Measure the application I/O size, queue depth and throughput before assuming a published maximum is attainable end to end.
